real_conflicts: Shifting the title block to the left or right third (Composition Verdict) creates a disjointed layout that fails to anchor the viewer. In a deep-sea context, the title must act as the central focal point—the 'eye' of the storm or the primary light source—rather than a sidebar element.

Removing the rigid wireframe sphere entirely (Composition Verdict) eliminates the necessary structural contrast. The brief asks for 'scientific curiosity'; the sphere provides the 'scientific' grid against which the organic typography and bioluminescence can rebel. Removing it makes the design purely abstract and loses the 'museum' credibility.
accepted: Applying a vertical gradient to the headline text (fading from white to dark blue) to simulate the diminishing light of the deep ocean.
Applying a soft, colored outer-glow effect to the text to integrate it with the bioluminescent lines, making the words feel like they are emitting light.
concession: I concede that the current flat grey color is a failure of integration. The text must not just sit on the background; it must participate in the lighting environment. I agree that the text needs to be treated as a light-emitting object.
compromise: We will keep the title centered to maintain the 'monumental' weight of the exhibition, but we will apply the proposed vertical gradient and glow effects. Crucially, we will layer the text *over* the wireframe sphere but *under* the foreground bioluminescent tendrils. This creates a 'sandwich' effect where the text is physically embedded in the environment, illuminated from within, rather than floating on top.
nonnegotiable: The headline 'BELOW THE LAST LIGHT' must remain the dominant visual anchor of the composition, retaining its scale and central positioning to ensure the poster functions as a unified statement rather than a scattered collection of elements.
